figures.shows: Schematic of the experiment: a feature vector x (for example a spoken vowel) is encoded by an SLM in the phases of the adiabatic frequency conversion (AFC) pump; one of four optical inputs (a squeezed vacuum from an OPA, b coherent state, c thermal state, d supercontinuum from a highly nonlinear fiber) enters the optical reservoir; an EMCCD camera behind a diffraction grating records frames from which a covariance matrix or a mean-field vector is computed and sent to a linear classifier.
figures.confirmed_by: We study physical RC using an optical reservoir that acts as a quantum reservoir when given a quantum state as a resource input

figures.shows: For each optical input with no data encoded: 100 consecutive EMCCD frames over 512 pixels (wavelength about 578 nm to about 657 nm) with the mean photon number per pixel as a purple line, and the covariance matrix. Squeezed vacuum (covariance colour scale about 0 to about 0.2) shows a diagonal and an anti-diagonal; supercontinuum (scale about 0 to about 1.0) shows discrete off-diagonal blocks; coherent and thermal (scale about 0 to about 0.05) show only a short central diagonal segment. The coherent and thermal mean fields are narrow peaks near about 619 nm, the squeezed and supercontinuum mean fields are broad.
figures.confirmed_by: Examples of the mean fields and covariance matrices that we observed are shown in Fig. 2 for each of the four types

figures.shows: Moons and blobs synthetic datasets. (a) Protocol schematic. (b.i, c.i) raw two-feature data with linear-SVM decision regions, titled Linear-kernel SVM Accuracy 70.2% (moons, four classes) and 68.8% (blobs, five classes). (b.ii, c.ii) test accuracy (y, about 37 to about 100%) against number of classes (x, two to four for moons, two to five for blobs) with a covariance-matrix feature vector for squeezed (violet), coherent (red), thermal (green) and supercontinuum (cyan) inputs and the linear-classifier line (dashed black); (b.iii, c.iii) the same with the mean-field vector. Moons covariance: squeezed about 97, about 87, about 83; coherent about 97, about 87, about 79; thermal about 89, about 67, about 55; supercontinuum about 69, about 49, about 37. Moons mean field at four classes: squeezed about 70, coherent about 80. Blobs covariance at five classes: squeezed about 80, coherent about 77, thermal about 70, supercontinuum about 68; blobs mean field at five classes: squeezed about 69, coherent about 73.
figures.confirmed_by: The classification accuracies obtained for the moons and blobs datasets using the covariance matrix and the mean-field vectors are shown in Fig. 3 in Panels b and c.

figures.shows: Spoken-vowel task. (a) test accuracy (y, 0 to 100%) against dataset size (x, about 30 to about 260) for experimental squeezed (violet, about 96 at the largest size), experimental coherent (red, about 88) and simulated coherent (orange, about 91), covariance feature vector. (b) accuracy against detected mean photon number (x up to about 2.5 times ten to the sixth): squeezed about 97, coherent about 88, simulated coherent about 92 at the largest value; inset confusion matrix with 66 of 70 test samples on the diagonal. papers.what_it_is: An experimental study that uses a frequency-multiplexed squeezed-light photonic device with more than 400 modes as a quantum reservoir computer for classification (synthetic datasets, spoken vowels, MNIST), comparing covariance and mean-field readouts and squeezed against classical light inputs.

assertions.value: The authors report experiments in which they used a frequency-multiplexed Gaussian boson sampler with more than 400 modes as the reservoir in quantum reservoir computing, evaluated on benchmark tasks including spoken-vowels classification and MNIST handwritten-digit classification.
quotes: Here we report on experiments in which we used a frequencymultiplexed GBS with > 400 modes as the reservoir in the quantum-machine-learning approach of quantum reservoir computing.
We evaluated the accuracy of our GBS-based reservoir computer on a variety of benchmark tasks, including spoken-vowels classification and MNIST handwritten-digit classification.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the paper's scope.

assertions.value: The authors state that using squeezed light consistently resulted in the highest (or tied highest, for simple tasks) accuracies among the optical inputs tested.
quotes: We found that using squeezed light consistently resulted in the highest (or tied highest, for simple tasks) accuracies.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one experimental study; the gap to coherent light is within error bars.
assertions.reader_inference: Section I footnote 7 and Section IV B (pp.3, 13) say the gap to coherent light is within statistical uncertainty.

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not report a full solution to the grand challenge of finding a practical application for which GBS provides a quantum advantage over all possible classical methods, but address part of it by exploring an application where GBS can perform the desired tasks well and experimentally provides an advantage over a classicalized version of their apparatus.
quotes: In this paper, we will not report a full solution to this grand challenge of finding a practical application for which GBS provides a quantum advantage
experimentally provides an advantage over a classicalized version of our experimental apparatus.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit on its own claims in Section I.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing prior work, that a commercial trapped-ion quantum processor reached a prediction accuracy of about 78% on MNIST handwritten-digit classification, while the classical state of the art from 1998 was about 99%.
quotes: Ref. [17] reported a prediction accuracy of ∼78% on MNIST handwritten-digit classification using a commercial trapped-ion quantum processor, while the classical state-of-the-art for the same task from 1998 was ∼99% [18].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to cited references.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing prior work, that training a classical classifier in quantum reservoir computing is far easier than training a quantum system, needing far fewer executions of the quantum system and not suffering from barren plateaus.
quotes: training a classical classifier is far easier than training a quantum system, needing far fewer executions of the quantum system (reservoir) and not suffering from barren plateaus [23].
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement the paper attributes to a cited reference.

assertions.value: The authors state that a useful quantum advantage can only result if the QRC achieves better performance on one or more practical machine-learning tasks than all alternative classical machine-learning methods, which is both hard to achieve and hard to prove, and that they do not address how to achieve quantum advantage in these experiments.
quotes: a useful quantum advantage can only result if the QRC is capable of achieving better performance on one or more practical machine-learning tasks than all alternative classical machine-learning methods—which is both hard to achieve, and hard to prove
we don’t address the question of how to achieve quantum advantage in the experiments reported in this paper
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope in Section I.

assertions.value: The authors describe the experimental reservoir as having three stages: generation of more than 400 modes of squeezed light, a programmable frequency-domain beamsplitter unitary through which classical data are input, and measurement by frequency-resolved photodetection used to estimate mean photon number per mode and two-body correlations between modes.
quotes: it comprises three stages, which we will explain further in the next section: (1) generation of > 400 modes of squeezed light; (2) frequency-domain-beamsplitter unitary evolution, where the beamsplitter unitary is programmable
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of its apparatus.

assertions.value: The authors state that they tested the quantum reservoir with several multiclass classification tasks, two standard machine-learning tests on synthetic data for nonlinear classifiers and two on real-world data (spoken-vowel and handwritten-digit classification).
